## Beginning to Manage the Project

:::{.callout-tip icon="false" collapse="false"}
### {{< fa brain >}} Learning Objectives

After completing this topic you will be able to: 

- <u>Explain</u> how to set up a project in GitHub
- <u>Describe</u> some benefits/drawbacks of different project management views
- <u>Draft</u> a plan for your own project using one of those tools

:::

Once your team goals and the necessary steps are agreed on, it becomes much easier to build a project plan that clarifies the timeline and team member responsibilities. Especially with limited-term projects such as ours, a Gantt chart can be a particularly valuable way to map out project dependencies and responsibilities. With each task arranged on a timeline, spotting hidden dependencies and unrealistic workloads becomes much easier.

A robust support infrastructure exists for the project management profession -- including formal training and a multitude of (often pricey) apps.
But for the job of managing research collaborations, we've found that the single most important factor is whether your collaborators will use the system.
For that to happen, they must have easy access to it, ideally without setting up a new account and as part of something they already do every day.

### Anatomy of an issue

If you're already working in GitHub or GitLab to collaborate on code, why not take advantage of GitHub's project management capabilities?
In GitHub, issues from your repos can be assigned to projects (which sit at a level above repos), allowing an overarching view of all the tasks associated with a project. Issues can also be created in the project itself.

Both kinds of issues can be assigned to individuals, marked with topical tags, and assigned start and due dates.
Many non-coders are also able to access and make good use of Gitub Projects through the web interface, which allows them to comment, raise questions, and take on tasks in the same interface as coders.

### Different views for different goals

Once once you have a few issues in your project, you'll find that GitHub Projects (and many other project management tools) offer multiple views to help guide your work and decision-making. The examples below draw from the repository we used to organize the first iteration of this course.

KanBan-style boards are often most intuitive, giving you a quick way to assess what is most urgent.

![A KanBan view of SSECR 2024 Project Board](topics/images/image_github-project.png){fig-alt="A series of vertical boards labelled back burner, inqueue, active progress, waiting, and done, with cards for specific tasks and individuals and due dates assigned" .lightbox}

The "roadmap" view let's you lay out your whole project with estimated start and end dates for various activities. It functions like an interactive Gantt chart, where issues can by dragged forward and back in time and the issue's start or end date will adjust accordingly. The stack of issues can also be sorted by start date, target date, topic tags or assigned collaborator.

![Gantt Chart Example using GitHub Projects](topics/images/image_github-gantt.png){fig-alt="A series of overlapping horizontal colored bars represents the active work periods for several critical project tasks" .lightbox}

The "sliced tasks view" allows each collaborator to see their own assigned tasks, which is very helpful when you  want to be sure you're delivering on your commitments.

![Filter by your own tasks to keep yourself accountable](topics/images/proj-mgmt-my-tasks.png){fig-alt="kanban board filtered down to only tasks assigned to the logged in user red circles highlight the my tasks tab and the filter criteria" .lightbox}

Another way to quickly access similar information is to filter the issues in your repository that are assigned to an individual.

![Repository issues can be used in a similar way](topics/images/proj-mgmt-issue-assigned.png){fig-alt="an issue list, filtered by the assigned user" .lightbox}

In the following activity, we'll ask you to think through the major steps you need to accomplish, break them into manageable sub-tasks, set time-bound goals, and assign tasks. This won't solve every project management challenge you face, but if you can maintain it at a reasonable level, it will help keep you on track, know who committed to what, and reduce bottlenecks. We've included a google sheet version of the Gantt chart, but recommend that you focus on doing it in GitHub.

::::{.callout-warning icon="false"}
### {{<fa rocket >}} Activity: Develop a Project Timeline/Gantt Chart (30 minutes)

As a project group, work through the following prompts.

Instructions are included for using either GitHub or a Google sheet template to complete a project Gantt chart. GitHub has more capabilities, especially for accessing individual task lists, but the Google Sheet template is included in case group members are not yet comfortable with GitHub.

:::{.panel-tabset}
    
### GitHub Project

1. Go to your project repository and find the project that has been created for you (top center menu)
    - It will open in a Kanban Board view
2. Begin adding tasks/issues (bottom of each list). Click on the task title to open it and add a brief description
    - A nice touch here is to add a checklist of subtasks
3. Choose task leads and add them to each task card (supporting group members can also be added)
4. Add approximate start dates and target end dates for each task
5. When you have most of your major tasks entered, switch to the roadmap view and shift the timelines as needed by extending the boxes or dragging them forward or back
6. Review the chart
    - What appear to be the bottlenecks? How could you mitigate them?
    - Can subgroups work simultaneously on different sub-projects?
    - Do you need to think about re-scoping the project?

### Google Sheet Template

1. Access the [**Google sheet template**](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1VtbsyTtJE-clviTAjtDnXM1GvXP6JusDq06AVm8WOUI/edit?usp=sharing), and copy it into your project folder
    - The template has two tabs
    - The manual one requires you to update the dates and graphical representation separately, but is a little more intuitive to edit and allows you to change bar color by assigned task lead
    - The "basic" tab will update the graph when you update task dates
2. Working backwards from the end of May, estimate how long each task will take and enter it in the spreadsheet
3. Add or remove steps as needed for your proposed project
4. Choose task leads
    - They should expect to draw on other group members for assistance and feedback
5. Review the chart
    - What appear to be the bottlenecks?
    - How could you mitigate them?
    - Can subgroups work simultaneously on different sub-projects?
    - Do you need to think about re-scoping the project?
6. Revise task dates as needed    

:::

- Regardless of which tool you used, decide on a plan for checking in and updating the Gantt chart
    - Every group meeting? Every Monday? Once a month?
- After 30 minutes, return to whole group and discuss any insights or innovations

::::
